classification.difficultyReason: Uses diagonal-bisection and rectangle properties to prove the converse of Thales’ theorem.

content.prompt:
The converse of Thales’ theorem is established by proving the following result:

The midpoint of the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle is equidistant from the three vertices of the triangle.

Let $\triangle ABP$ be right-angled at $P$, and let $O$ be the midpoint of the hypotenuse $AB$. Draw $PO$ and produce it to $Q$ so that $PO=OQ$. Draw $AQ$ and $BQ$.

spec.description: Upright rectangle construction with solid original triangle ABP, dashed added sides and diagonal, midpoint ticks and a right-angle mark.
spec.mathematics: Angle BPA=90 degrees; AO=OB; PO=OQ; diagonals AB and PQ intersect at O. Two ticks mark AO and OB; three ticks mark PO and OQ.
spec.answerVisibility: Construction and givens only; no inferred equalities added.

answer.worked: $AO=OB$ because $O$ is the midpoint of $AB$, and $PO=OQ$ by construction. Thus diagonals $AB$ and $PQ$ bisect each other at $O$, so $APBQ$ is a parallelogram.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Hence, explain why $APBQ$ is a rectangle.

answer.short: It is a parallelogram with a right angle.
answer.worked: $\angle APB=90^\circ$ is given. A parallelogram with a right angle is a rectangle, so $APBQ$ is a rectangle.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Hence, explain why $AO=BO=PO$ and why the circle with diameter $AB$ passes through $P$.

answer.short: $AO=BO=PO$, since a rectangle’s diagonals are equal and bisect each other. The circle has centre $O$ and radius $OP$, so it passes through $P$.
answer.worked:
The diagonals of rectangle $APBQ$ are equal and bisect each other, so $AB=PQ$ and
$$AO=BO=\frac{AB}{2}=\frac{PQ}{2}=PO.$$
The circle with diameter $AB$ has centre $O$ and radius $AO$. Since $OP=AO$, the point $P$ lies on this circle.
